title: Fernando Mastrangelo’s Dyed-Sand Mirror Powerfully Reflects on Beauty, Materiality and the Politics of Place
summary: "The Divide" is part of an ambitious new exhibition now on display at Cristina Grajales Gallery.
body_markdown:
[The Divide , 2026, by Fernando Mastrangelo](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/mirrors/wall-mirrors/mirror-diptych-divide/id-f_52917542/)


As the market for contemporary design heated up in the first decade of this century, among the genre’s brightest stars was[Fernando Mastrangelo](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/fernando-mastrangelo/) , with his art-world cred (he had cut his teeth in the studio of[Matthew Barney](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/matthew-barney/) ) and bold exploration of materials (sand and salt, in particular). He also paved the way for other designers, promoting their work through his Brooklyn studio and website. Then, Mastrangelo stepped away, moving upstate, to Hudson.


[Fernando Mastrangelo](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/fernando-mastrangelo/) stands next to the Bloodland table from his “Territories” exhibition, which is now on view at[Cristina Grajales](https://www.1stdibs.com/dealers/cristina-grajales-gallery/) ‘ Tribeca gallery. Portrait by Joe Kramm


But now, he’s back — in a big way, although with a smaller studio, fully focused on his own practice — collaborating with powerhouse dealer[Cristina Grajales](https://www.1stdibs.com/dealers/cristina-grajales-gallery/) , who over the years has championed the work of such designer/artist supernovas as Sheila Hicks,[Robert Wilson](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/robert-wilson/) and[Michele Oka Doner](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/michele-oka-doner/) . At Grajales’s Tribeca gallery until February 1, 2027, you can catch “Territories,” a gorgeous exhibition of Mastrangelo’s latest body of work — tables, case pieces, lighting and wall-hung artworks, all cast from dyed sand and crushed glass — which brings landscape “painting” into conversation with contemporary concerns about geopolitics, environmentalism and belonging.


This pair of tables, called The Divide (01,02), are crafted from sand and powdered glass.


Among the one-dimensional pieces featured in the show, a standout is[The Divide](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/mirrors/wall-mirrors/mirror-diptych-divide/id-f_52917542/) , a diptych that introduces mirror-polished bronze into the material mix. “ *The Divide* exemplifies the direction I’m taking my practice: bringing material, form and meaning closer together,” Mastrangelo says. “The sand and glass build the landscape, while the separation between the panels becomes part of its meaning. I want the beauty of the work to draw people in and give them a reason to stay with more difficult questions about territory, ownership and our relationship to the land.”


The[mirrors](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/mirrors/wall-mirrors/mirror-diptych-divide/id-f_52917542/) , which can be hung multiple ways, bring landscape “painting” into conversation with contemporary concerns about geopolitics, environmentalism and belonging.


That’s an ambitious program, but it embodies the sort of complex thinking that has always driven Mastrangelo’s practice. “In both my sculpture and furniture,” he says, “I’m working toward pieces where the ideas are inseparable from how they’re made.”
